title: Polaris DevTools - customer story interview #1 (integration + perf/cost results)
summary: Customer story interview focused on Polaris DevTools’ rollout of Redwood Hosted API for chat + code assistant features. Team described initial integration (hours/days), routing from previous providers, and the practical impact of Redwood batching/caching recommendations on unit cost and p95 latency. Discussed what they’re comfortable sharing publicly (ranges vs exact metrics), what developer experience elements mattered (docs, SDK parity, streaming reliability, observability), and constraints (peak traffic bursts, multi-tenant isolation expectations, and incident communication). Agreed on story angle: time-to-value + production economics without sacrificing reliability.
topics: Background: Polaris DevTools product and LLM feature set
Migration timeline and integration details (SDK, streaming, retries, rate limits)
Performance: latency, throughput, tail behavior during spikes
Cost: batching, cache hit rate, prompt/token controls
Developer experience feedback (docs, examples, console, support)
What can be published: logo/quote approvals, metric ranges, wording
next_steps: Redwood (Ethan) to send a short follow-up doc with proposed narrative + 3–5 candidate quotes for review
Polaris (Maya) to confirm internal approver for logo + quote and preferred review window
Redwood (Markus) to share a simplified architecture diagram draft (hosted API + caching/batching) for customer validation
Polaris (Jon/Elena) to provide one screenshot or redacted snippet of internal dashboard showing latency trend (optional)
Schedule interview #2 focused on business impact + rollout learnings (late Oct)
action_items: Ethan: Draft story outline + quote options and send to Maya by 2025-10-17

transcript:
Meeting: Polaris DevTools - customer story interview #1 (integration + perf/cost results)
Recorded by Fireflies.ai
Date: 2025-10-14
Start time: 10:02 AM PT
Duration: 43 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Ethan Wallace (Marketing), Soojin Lee (Product Marketing), Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering)
Polaris DevTools: Maya Patel (Head of Product), Jon Park (Staff Engineer), Elena Rossi (ML Engineer)

---

[00:00] Ethan Wallace: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is the first customer story interview. Goal is basically to get the raw material—timeline, what you built, what changed with Redwood, and what you’d be comfortable putting in a public case study.

[00:18] Maya Patel: Yep. Sounds good.

[00:20] Soojin Lee: And we’ll keep it pretty conversational. If we get into stuff you don’t want quoted, just say “off the record” and we’ll flag it.

[00:30] Jon Park: Great.

[00:31] Elena Rossi: Yeah.

[00:34] Ethan Wallace: Quick intros for the recording. I’m Ethan, I write/edit the case studies. Soojin runs messaging. Markus is solutions engineering.

[00:42] Maya Patel: I’m Maya, product lead at Polaris. We build devtools—our main product is like a “workspace copilot” inside CI and IDE contexts.

[00:52] Jon Park: Jon, staff engineer, I own our inference gateway and like the runtime plumbing.

[00:58] Elena Rossi: Elena, ML engineer. I do prompt evals, model testing, and—uh—anything that touches embeddings and reranking.

[01:07] Ethan Wallace: Awesome. Maybe to start, Maya, can you give the 60-second “what Polaris does” and where LLMs show up?

[01:15] Maya Patel: Sure. Polaris helps engineering teams understand and change large codebases. We have a code search layer, and then an assistant that can answer “where is this function used” or “why did this build fail,” that kind of thing. LLMs show up in three places: chat Q&A, doc/code summarization, and then a smaller “explain this diff” thing in pull requests.

[01:39] Soojin Lee: Are you primarily doing that inside the product, or do you also offer an API?

[01:43] Maya Patel: Mostly inside the product. We have some API endpoints but it’s not like a platform.

[01:49] Ethan Wallace: Great. And when did you start working with Redwood?

[01:53] Jon Park: We started a serious eval… I want to say early June? We had prototypes earlier in the year, but the “we need to pick a provider and ship it” was June.

[02:05] Elena Rossi: June-ish, yeah. We had a rough patch with tail latency at the time.

[02:12] Ethan Wallace: Okay, perfect segue. What was the setup before Redwood? You don’t need to name names if you don’t want, but just describe.

[02:20] Jon Park: We were on a mix. For the prototype we used OpenAI. Then we tried one of the “open model hosted” providers—Together, and also we played with Bedrock because enterprise customers asked.

[02:34] Maya Patel: Yeah, and it was a lot of “it works on Tuesday and then Thursday it’s different.”

[02:39] Soojin Lee: Different like quality, or performance?

[02:42] Maya Patel: Performance and reliability. Like rate limits, weird timeouts. And quality drift sometimes, but mainly it was the serving side.

[02:51] Jon Park: To be fair, we also were not very disciplined. We’d change prompts and settings, then blame the provider. But the consistent pain was p95 and p99 swings, especially during US business hours.

[03:05] Markus Klein: That’s helpful. When you say swings, are we talking like 20% or like multiples?

[03:10] Jon Park: Multiples. Like a normal p95 around… I think 1.6 to 2 seconds end-to-end for the chat response to start streaming, and then on bad days it would be 4, 5 seconds before the first token.

[03:24] Elena Rossi: And when you’re doing “explain this stack trace,” users just bounce. They think it’s broken.

[03:31] Ethan Wallace: Understood. For the story, we like to anchor on a few “before/after” metrics. We can do ranges if exact numbers are sensitive. Would you be comfortable with that kind of framing?

[03:43] Maya Patel: Ranges, yes. Exact dollars probably no. Exact volume, no. But “cut latency in half” or “improved tail latency” is fine.

[03:54] Soojin Lee: Got it. We can also phrase as “reduced p95 from ~2s to under 1s” sort of thing, if you’re comfortable.

[04:01] Maya Patel: That’s probably okay, yeah.

[04:06] Ethan Wallace: Nice. Let’s talk integration. Jon, how hard was it to adopt Redwood’s API compared to what you had?

[04:14] Jon Park: Pretty easy. We already had an abstraction layer because we were switching providers. So Redwood basically became another backend. The main changes were: we switched streaming handling because Redwood’s SSE format was slightly different than one of the others.

[04:30] Markus Klein: Different like event names, or chunking?

[04:33] Jon Park: Chunking and the “final” message. We had one bug where we’d treat the last chunk as empty and we’d cut off the answer. That was our bug.

[04:43] Elena Rossi: Also we started using your “structured output” mode for one internal tool. That required prompt tweaks.

[04:51] Soojin Lee: How long from “we decided” to “it’s in production”?

[04:57] Jon Park: Initial integration was like… half a day? To get a basic call working. Then production readiness—retries, timeouts, tracing, dashboards—maybe two weeks.

[05:10] Maya Patel: The biggest time wasn’t coding, it was “we need to be confident.” Like running evals and doing a staged rollout.

[05:18] Ethan Wallace: That’s a good point. Can you describe the rollout? Was it all users at once or…

[05:23] Maya Patel: We did internal dogfooding first, then 10% of paid accounts, then 50%, then everyone. The gating was mostly “are we seeing regressions in support tickets.”

[05:36] Elena Rossi: And we had an eval set of like 200 prompts. Not huge, but representative.

[05:43] Markus Klein: Were you using Redwood for both chat and embeddings, or just chat?

[05:48] Elena Rossi: Chat primarily. Embeddings we still do elsewhere because of some legacy index stuff. But we’re considering moving because it’s annoying having two vendors.

[06:00] Ethan Wallace: Okay. On the Redwood side, are you on Hosted API only, or did you look at Dedicated?

[06:05] Maya Patel: Hosted API. We’re not big enough to justify Dedicated yet.

[06:10] Jon Park: Also we’re multi-tenant and we didn’t need isolated hardware, we just needed predictable performance.

[06:17] Soojin Lee: What tipped you from “evaluate” to “ship with Redwood”?

[06:22] Maya Patel: Two things. One was the latency consistency. And the other was, frankly, your team was very responsive. Like we’d ask “why is this request slow” and you’d show us in the console, like token timing, not just “it’s fine.”

[06:39] Elena Rossi: Yeah the token-level breakdown is useful. It’s like, okay, we are prompting too long, not “the model is slow.”

[06:48] Markus Klein: Ha, yes. Prompt bloat is real.

[06:52] Ethan Wallace: Let’s dig into the improvements you saw. Jon you mentioned first-token p95. What’s the “after” range?

[07:00] Jon Park: After Redwood, we’re typically under a second to first token for our main chat endpoint. Not always, but… p95 is under 1s most days.

[07:13] Soojin Lee: That’s great. Any story around p99 or those “bad days”?

[07:18] Jon Park: The big thing is we don’t have those 5-second first token spikes anymore. We still see slower responses if we hit rate limits on our side or if someone sends like a giant context.

[07:30] Elena Rossi: Or if the retrieval returns a million lines. Which is our problem.

[07:35] Ethan Wallace: (laughs) Classic.

[07:37] Markus Klein: Did you end up using any specific Redwood features to get there? Like caching, batching, or model selection.

[07:44] Jon Park: Two main levers. One, we turned on prompt prefix caching—or I’m going to say it wrong, KV cache reuse. We have a system prompt that’s identical across requests, and we were paying for it every time before.

[08:00] Markus Klein: Yep, prefix/KV caching.

[08:03] Jon Park: Right. And then second, we adjusted batching. Initially we were paranoid batching would hurt latency, but your Optimize recommendations were like “batch size 4” for our traffic pattern, and that actually didn’t change p95 much but improved throughput.

[08:21] Elena Rossi: And cost.

[08:22] Ethan Wallace: That’s one of the key story angles we want: improved unit economics without making it slower. Can you quantify cost impact?

[08:31] Maya Patel: Again, ranges. We saw something like 30 to 40% reduction in cost per… per output. Our finance team cares per active user per month, but roughly it mapped to per-token cost reduction.

[08:45] Jon Park: Yeah, it’s complicated because we also changed prompts and we started truncating context more aggressively.

[08:51] Soojin Lee: That’s fine. We can be honest: “Combination of Redwood optimization + prompt discipline.”

[08:58] Elena Rossi: I’d say Redwood made it easy to see where waste was. Like before, it was guesswork.

[09:06] Markus Klein: Did you change models during this? Or keep same-ish model class?

[09:10] Elena Rossi: We tested a few. We ended up on one of the open instruction models in your catalog. We started with a bigger one, but for the “explain a diff” use case we dropped down a size.

[09:24] Ethan Wallace: For public writeup, can we name the model?

[09:27] Maya Patel: Probably not. Just say “open-source instruction model” or “Redwood’s curated open model.”

[09:33] Soojin Lee: Works.

[09:36] Ethan Wallace: Let’s talk developer experience. What did you like and what was annoying? Real feedback is helpful.

[09:44] Jon Park: Docs were good. The API surface is straightforward. SDK-wise, the Node client was fine. We did hit one issue where the retry behavior wasn’t obvious. We weren’t sure if we should retry on 429s versus backoff.

[10:01] Markus Klein: Yeah, that’s a common question. We can clarify in docs.

[10:05] Jon Park: The console is nice. Being able to slice by route and see p95 and error rates. I liked that you can see streaming errors distinctly.

[10:16] Elena Rossi: For me, biggest win was the “cost breakdown” and the suggestions. Like, “your prompt is 9k tokens and your completion is 200” and you’re like okay, we have to fix retrieval.

[10:30] Maya Patel: Support experience was honestly the standout. Not in a fluffy way—like it felt like you had engineers who understood the problem.

[10:39] Soojin Lee: Is there a specific moment you remember? Like a ticket or a late night?

[10:44] Jon Park: Yeah, during the first week of rollout we saw intermittent timeouts. We sent logs, and Markus—well, someone—jumped on a call and basically showed it was our client timing out at 10 seconds while streaming was still active.

[11:00] Markus Klein: I remember that.

[11:01] Jon Park: And you gave us a recommended timeout config for “time to first token” versus “overall stream duration.”

[11:09] Ethan Wallace: That’s a great anecdote.

[11:12] Elena Rossi: Also, you had a status page update when there was a regional hiccup. That matters to us.

[11:20] Ethan Wallace: On reliability—did you implement any fallback routing, like multiple models or regions?

[11:27] Jon Park: Lightly. We have a fallback to a second model variant, but we don’t use it often. We mostly rely on Redwood being stable.

[11:37] Markus Klein: Okay. And did you configure rate limits or quotas?

[11:41] Jon Park: Yes. We set per-tenant quotas in our gateway. On Redwood side, we set org-level limits to avoid surprise bills.

[11:52] Maya Patel: We needed that for finance predictability.

[11:56] Soojin Lee: For the story, we also like including a “what constraints made this hard” section. What were the non-negotiables?

[12:04] Maya Patel: Non-negotiables were: streaming must feel snappy, and data handling must be reasonable. We’re not in healthcare, but our customers paste proprietary code, so we need confidence around data retention and not training on it.

[12:20] Ethan Wallace: Yep. And Redwood policy is no training on customer prompts by default.

[12:24] Jon Park: Right. We also needed consistent behavior across time zones. We have EU customers too.

[12:32] Markus Klein: Did you use a specific region?

[12:34] Jon Park: Mostly US West. EU users hit it too; it’s okay. We might add EU region later.

[12:43] Elena Rossi: For EU we’re more concerned about latency than legal, right now.

[12:48] Ethan Wallace: Okay. Let’s capture some implementation detail we can turn into an architecture diagram. Jon can you describe the high-level flow?

[12:57] Jon Park: Sure. Client in the IDE calls our backend. Backend calls our retrieval service—vector search + some heuristics. Then we assemble prompt, call Redwood chat completion endpoint with streaming. We stream tokens back to the client.

[13:14] Markus Klein: Do you do tool calling or function calling?

[13:17] Jon Park: Not via Redwood tool calling yet. We do a homegrown “actions” system. But it’s basically the same: the model returns JSON-ish and then we execute.

[13:28] Elena Rossi: We might switch to formal tool calling because it’s less brittle.

[13:35] Soojin Lee: If we include “structured output support” in the story, is that accurate?

[13:40] Elena Rossi: Yes, but limited. We used it for one internal thing: generating a triage summary with fixed fields.

[13:48] Ethan Wallace: Great. Now the tricky part: metrics. You already said p95 to first token under a second. Can we say “50% reduction” or do you prefer “roughly cut in half”?

[14:00] Maya Patel: “Roughly cut in half” is safer.

[14:03] Ethan Wallace: And cost: “30–40% reduction in per-request cost” or “meaningful reduction in unit cost”?

[14:10] Maya Patel: We can do “30–40% reduction in inference spend for this feature.” But I want to review the exact wording.

[14:18] Soojin Lee: Absolutely. We’ll provide an approval draft.

[14:23] Markus Klein: Also, make sure it’s attributed as “Polaris observed,” not like Redwood guaranteeing.

[14:27] Soojin Lee: Yes, we’ll keep it grounded.

[14:31] Ethan Wallace: Any other quantitative-ish things? Like throughput or uptime.

[14:36] Jon Park: Uptime improved, but I don’t have a number. We had fewer incidents. But it’s fuzzy because some were on us.

[14:45] Elena Rossi: We did see fewer “model returned nonsense” but that’s quality, not uptime.

[14:52] Maya Patel: Another metric is “time to ship.” Like we went from “prototype” to “GA” in, what, a month? Maybe six weeks.

[15:01] Jon Park: Yeah, about six weeks from serious evaluation to full rollout.

[15:06] Ethan Wallace: That’s great for developer-first angle.

[15:10] Soojin Lee: Speaking of, what about the API experience felt developer-first to you? Or what language would you use.

[15:18] Jon Park: It’s predictable. Errors are understandable. Rate limit responses tell you what to do. And streaming doesn’t randomly break.

[15:29] Elena Rossi: Also, you’re not hiding everything. Like, I can actually see latency breakdowns. With other providers it’s just “trust us.”

[15:39] Maya Patel: Yeah. And you didn’t force us into a giant enterprise contract. We could start self-serve and then talk later.

[15:48] Ethan Wallace: Great. On the flip side, anything you’d improve?

[15:53] Jon Park: Documentation around “best practices” for timeouts and retries with streaming. And maybe examples for multi-tenant quota handling.

[16:05] Elena Rossi: More guidance on evals would be helpful. Like a reference harness.

[16:10] Markus Klein: Noted. We do have an eval harness internally; maybe DevEx can publish more.

[16:16] Soojin Lee: Okay. I’m going to ask for a quote from each of you, and then later we’ll send it back for approval. Maya, if you had to summarize why Redwood, what would you say?

[16:28] Maya Patel: “Redwood let us ship an AI assistant that feels fast and reliable, without the team spending months tuning infrastructure.” Something like that.

[16:37] Ethan Wallace: Great. Jon?

[16:40] Jon Park: “The integration was straightforward, and the performance was consistent—especially the time to first token.”

[16:47] Soojin Lee: Elena?

[16:49] Elena Rossi: “We reduced cost and improved responsiveness by using Redwood’s caching and batching recommendations, and we could actually measure the impact.”

[17:01] Ethan Wallace: Excellent. We’ll polish but keep meaning.

[17:06] Markus Klein: Quick technical check: when you say caching, we should say prefix caching/KV reuse, not like response cache, unless you did response cache.

[17:13] Jon Park: Correct, not response cache.

[17:15] Elena Rossi: Yeah, prefix.

[17:18] Ethan Wallace: Good catch. Now, any sensitive areas we should avoid in the writeup? Like customer names, security posture.

[17:27] Maya Patel: Avoid naming our enterprise customers. Avoid volume numbers. Avoid model name. Also, avoid anything that sounds like we’re endorsing open model X.

[17:38] Soojin Lee: Understood.

[17:40] Ethan Wallace: Are you comfortable with your logo on the case study page?

[17:45] Maya Patel: Tentatively yes, subject to brand review. I need to loop in our comms person.

[17:53] Ethan Wallace: Great. We can share the consent form separately.

[17:57] Maya Patel: Yeah.

[18:00] Ethan Wallace: Let’s talk about the “moment of pain” that made this urgent. Was there a specific event? A launch? A customer escalation?

[18:09] Maya Patel: We had a beta customer who loved the feature but kept complaining it was slow. And that customer is pretty influential in our segment.

[18:18] Jon Park: And we had internal alerts. Our provider at the time had queueing, and our chat endpoint was hitting like 10+ seconds end-to-end sometimes.

[18:27] Elena Rossi: Also, we were spending too much. Like we were seeing bills and thinking “this will never scale.”

[18:35] Soojin Lee: That’s a strong narrative: “fast enough to delight, cheap enough to scale.”

[18:40] Maya Patel: Exactly.

[18:42] Ethan Wallace: Any detail on what changed the economics? Was it mainly batching/caching, or also model choice and prompt length.

[18:51] Elena Rossi: It’s all three. Model size downshift for some flows, prompt trimming, and then batching/caching.

[18:58] Jon Park: Redwood made batching easier because you had guidance. Previously, we were scared of it.

[19:05] Markus Klein: Did you change max tokens or stop sequences?

[19:08] Jon Park: We set max tokens lower for some actions. And we added “stop” tokens for code blocks.

[19:15] Elena Rossi: We also did “stream until answer complete” but cut off if it started rambling.

[19:21] Ethan Wallace: Nice. Okay. I want to make sure we have the timeline clearly. Let me repeat what I heard: serious evaluation started in June, integration was less than a day, production readiness two weeks, full rollout about six weeks. Is that right?

[19:36] Jon Park: Yes.

[19:37] Maya Patel: That’s right.

[19:39] Elena Rossi: Yep.

[19:41] Soojin Lee: And when did you go GA? Like when did you start marketing it.

[19:46] Maya Patel: Late July we announced to customers. August we made it default.

[19:52] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[19:55] Markus Klein: You mentioned you have an inference gateway. Did you have to do any special auth handling for Redwood keys?

[20:01] Jon Park: We rotate keys monthly. Redwood API keys fit into that. Nothing special.

[20:07] Markus Klein: Did you use organizations/projects separation?

[20:10] Jon Park: Yes, we have separate projects for staging and prod.

[20:14] Ethan Wallace: Good for “enterprise readiness” even though you’re on hosted.

[20:18] Soojin Lee: Do you have any “before Redwood” quote? Like what it felt like.

[20:24] Maya Patel: “We were spending more time debugging the inference layer than improving the product.”

[20:30] Ethan Wallace: That’s excellent.

[20:33] Elena Rossi: And “we couldn’t trust our metrics.” Like latency would change and we didn’t know if it was us.

[20:41] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[20:44] Markus Klein: For the diagram, I’ll propose something simple: IDE/client -> Polaris API -> Retrieval service -> Redwood API (streaming) -> back. Plus an optional box for caching/batching at Redwood. Does that reflect reality?

[20:58] Jon Park: Yes. Just don’t draw our internal infra too specifically.

[21:02] Markus Klein: Of course.

[21:04] Ethan Wallace: We’re at about half time. I want to spend the rest on approvals and what we publish.

[21:11] Maya Patel: Sure.

[21:12] Ethan Wallace: What’s your internal approval path? Brand, legal, product?

[21:18] Maya Patel: Brand/comms for logo and public quote. Legal if there’s a contract attached. Product sign-off from me.

[21:27] Soojin Lee: And review window—what’s realistic?

[21:31] Maya Patel: If you give us a week, we’re good. If it’s 48 hours, no.

[21:36] Ethan Wallace: Great. We’ll plan for 5 business days.

[21:41] Ethan Wallace: Any restrictions on referencing Redwood by name as your provider?

[21:46] Maya Patel: No, we can say we use Redwood.

[21:49] Ethan Wallace: Great. And you’re open to reference calls too, or just case study?

[21:55] Maya Patel: Reference calls are okay but limited. Like maybe one per month. And we want to know the prospect context.

[22:03] Soojin Lee: That’s consistent with our program guardrails.

[22:07] Jon Park: And we’d rather talk to technical folks, not like procurement.

[22:12] Ethan Wallace: Makes sense.

[22:14] Markus Klein: If a prospect asks “how did you do multi-tenant isolation,” are you comfortable discussing that?

[22:20] Jon Park: At a high level yes. But no details about our internal security. We can say we have per-tenant quotas and we don’t log raw prompts.

[22:29] Elena Rossi: And no specific customer names.

[22:32] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[22:35] Soojin Lee: For the written story, we usually have sections: Challenge, Solution, Implementation, Results. Any “challenge” language you like?

[22:44] Maya Patel: Challenge was “we needed to ship a fast AI assistant without runaway costs, and we didn’t want to build an inference platform.”

[22:55] Ethan Wallace: Perfect.

[22:57] Elena Rossi: Also we needed consistency for user trust.

[23:01] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[23:03] Markus Klein: One more technical: are you using streaming on every request or only chat?

[23:09] Jon Park: Mostly chat. Summaries sometimes non-streaming.

[23:13] Markus Klein: Okay.

[23:16] Ethan Wallace: Did you end up using any Redwood features in the console for debugging? Like traces, request IDs.

[23:23] Jon Park: Yes, request IDs. We wired them into our logs. That was huge.

[23:30] Elena Rossi: We also used the “compare runs” thing—maybe that was a beta? Where you can see two prompts side by side.

[23:37] Markus Klein: That’s in Console under experiments, yeah.

[23:40] Soojin Lee: That’s a nice devex point.

[23:43] Ethan Wallace: Cool. Another piece: distribution. We might publish this on our docs site and as a PDF 1-pager. Are you okay with that?

[23:52] Maya Patel: Yes, as long as we approve final.

[23:55] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[23:57] Soojin Lee: Would you be open to a short quote from a named person (you, Maya), with title?

[24:04] Maya Patel: Yes. Title is fine. Again, approve exact quote.

[24:10] Ethan Wallace: Great.

[24:12] Markus Klein: If we mention “Optimize recommendations,” is that okay, or does it sound too salesy?

[24:18] Maya Patel: It’s fine if it’s described as “guidance on batching/caching settings.”

[24:24] Soojin Lee: We can phrase it like that.

[24:27] Ethan Wallace: Okay. Any concerns about being perceived as endorsing a vendor too strongly?

[24:34] Maya Patel: As long as it’s factual and not like “best in the world.”

[24:38] Ethan Wallace: We won’t do that.

[24:41] Ethan Wallace: Quick check: do you have any upcoming launch we could align timing with?

[24:47] Maya Patel: We’re launching a new “PR assistant” in November. But we don’t want to tie the story to that.

[24:54] Soojin Lee: Understood.

[24:56] Ethan Wallace: Great. Then we’ll aim to publish whenever approvals are done.

[25:02] Elena Rossi: One thing—if you include cost numbers, we’d prefer percentages.

[25:07] Ethan Wallace: Noted.

[25:09] Markus Klein: And for latency, we can say “p95 to first token under 1 second” and “reduced by about half.”

[25:15] Maya Patel: Yes.

[25:17] Ethan Wallace: Cool.

[25:19] Soojin Lee: Anything else you want to highlight that we haven’t asked? Like a surprising lesson.

[25:26] Jon Park: The lesson is: you can’t treat the provider as a black box. You need observability and you need to control prompts. Redwood helped with that.

[25:36] Elena Rossi: Another lesson: streaming UX matters more than average latency. Users judge “did it start immediately.”

[25:45] Maya Patel: And we learned to treat inference spend like a product metric, not just infra.

[25:52] Ethan Wallace: These are great. We’ll incorporate.

[25:55] Ethan Wallace: Okay, let’s wrap with next steps. We’ll draft a short outline and send you candidate quotes and the “metrics language” for review.

[26:05] Maya Patel: Great.

[26:06] Ethan Wallace: Markus will draft a simple architecture diagram and run it by Jon.

[26:11] Jon Park: Yep.

[26:12] Ethan Wallace: And then we’ll schedule interview #2 that’s more “business impact and rollout learnings.” Probably 30 minutes.

[26:20] Maya Patel: Works.

[26:22] Soojin Lee: Also, if you can think of one internal graph you can share—redacted—like latency trend over time, that’s super helpful. Totally optional.

[26:31] Jon Park: We might be able to do that. I’ll check.

[26:34] Elena Rossi: I can also share an eval summary, but it might be too in the weeds.

[26:39] Ethan Wallace: Even a “we used an eval set of ~200 prompts” is a good credibility point.

[26:44] Elena Rossi: Okay.

[26:46] Ethan Wallace: Any final questions for us?

[26:49] Maya Patel: Just confirm—this isn’t going live without our approval.

[26:53] Ethan Wallace: Correct. Nothing public without written approval.

[26:56] Maya Patel: Great.

[26:58] Jon Park: And for reference calls, we’ll need like a short brief of who the prospect is.

[27:04] Soojin Lee: Yep, we have a template for that.

[27:07] Ethan Wallace: Awesome. Thanks everyone.

[27:10] Maya Patel: Thanks.

[27:11] Jon Park: Thanks.

[27:12] Elena Rossi: Bye.
